sections.html:
Montgomery Township sits in Montgomery County in the Philadelphia suburbs, along PA 309 near the Bucks County line. It covers 10.63 square miles of land, all of it developed or developing, and the 2020 census counted 25,862 residents. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 26,210.

Its downtown is Montgomery Square on PA 309, and the postal community of Montgomeryville carries ZIP code 19454. The township also includes parts of villages shared with neighbors: Colmar and Fortuna with Hatfield Township, and Christy and Eureka with Bucks County and Horsham Township. Little Neshaminy Creek drains most of the area, which puts it in the Delaware watershed. Neighbors include Horsham, Lower Gwynedd and Upper Gwynedd townships, the borough of Lansdale and Hatfield Township, plus New Britain and Warrington townships across the line in Bucks County.

The township was incorporated on May 17, 1714, making it one of the older municipalities in the county. Alexander Edwards, one of the first settlers, was born in Wales and wrote "of Montgomery" in his will before his death in 1712. Many Welsh families settled in this part of old Philadelphia County, and the county that formed on September 10, 1784 was probably named for Montgomeryshire in Wales. The Knapp Farm was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1976.

The population curve explains the housing stock. The township had 850 residents in 1930 and 2,700 in 1960, then 5,718 in 1980 and 12,179 in 1990. It reached 22,025 in 2000. Most houses are therefore from the 1980s through the 2000s, with fewer than 30 years of growth since the last big wave of building. Many sit in homeowner association communities, and the township's residential permit checklist asks for association approval in specific developments.

About 92 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, and 19.3 percent were born outside the United States. Asian residents make up 22.2 percent of the population. For a seller, that means a stable pool of local buyers and a market where the typical home value is close to half a million dollars, so small price gaps translate into large dollar amounts.

sections.h2: What roads and transit connect Montgomery Township?
sections.html:
Several major routes cross the township, which is why it is often marketed as a commuter location:

  • U.S. 202 runs southwest to northeast through the center on a parkway-style road.
  • PA 309 runs north to south on Bethlehem Pike through Montgomery Square.
  • PA 63 follows Welsh Road along the southwestern edge, and PA 152 passes through the eastern corner on Limekiln Pike.
  • PA 463 crosses on Cowpath Road and Horsham Road, and County Line Road marks part of the Bucks County boundary.

SEPTA runs Suburban Bus routes 94, 96 and 132 to Montgomery Mall. The Census Bureau puts mean travel time to work at 29.0 minutes, which is longer than in most of Pennsylvania's smaller towns. The hardiness zone line between 6b and 7a runs along a ridge near Stump Road, and January averages about 29.9 degrees against 74.3 degrees in July, so gardens and landscaping differ a little across the township.

sections.h2: Does Montgomery Township require an inspection when a house is sold?
sections.html:
The township's fee schedule lists a Use and Occupancy permit for residential property only for new construction, at $150, with other occupancy permits aimed at manufactured homes and non-residential space. That means a resale of an existing single-family house does not appear to need a township resale certificate the way some Pennsylvania municipalities require. Call the Planning and Zoning Office at (215) 393-6920 to confirm for your address, since homeowner associations and your buyer's lender can add their own steps.

Permits still matter if you did work on the house. Decks, finished basements, re-roofing, sheds, fences and sign installations all need permits, and the township lists residential requirements and common permit projects on its website. Open permits or unpermitted work often come up during a buyer's inspection, so pull your permit history before you list. The township's Codes and Permits page is at 1001 Stump Road, Montgomeryville, and is open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

sections.h2: How do taxes, homestead and appeals work for a Montgomery Township seller?
sections.html:
The Montgomery County Board of Assessment Appeals sets assessed values for county, municipal and school taxes. Annual appeals have to be filed by August 1 of the year before the tax year in question, and the same date applies to exemption applications. The deadline exists because appeals must be decided by October 31 and the rolls must reach owners and taxing districts by November 15.

The Homestead and Farmstead Exclusion lowers the taxable value of a primary residence. Applications filed by March 1 take effect for school taxes the following July 1, and December 15 is the deadline for municipal relief in participating municipalities. One rule matters to sellers: when a property changes ownership, the exclusion is removed automatically, so the seller does not need to file anything and the buyer must apply again. A decision on an application can be appealed within 40 days.

The county's USPS notice also warns that mailed filings can be postmarked late, so ask for a hand-cancelled postmark or deliver the paper to the Norristown office.

sections.h2: What is the transfer tax and what disclosures apply in Montgomery Township?
sections.html:
The Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds states the realty transfer tax at 2 percent of the price. It collects the tax at recording, and an exemption needs a REV-183 Statement of Value from the Department of Revenue. The county also posts a common level ratio factor each July, and the factor for July 2026 through June 2027 is 3.36.

Pennsylvania's Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law, Chapter 73 of Title 68, requires a seller to complete a property disclosure statement and deliver it signed and dated before the buyer and seller sign an agreement of transfer. A seller is not required to investigate, but may not state anything known to be false or leave out a known material defect. If a disclosure becomes inaccurate before settlement, the seller must tell the buyer. A buyer has two years after settlement to sue for damages under the chapter.

sections.h2: What happens if taxes are unpaid, and what are the ways to sell?
sections.html:
The Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau holds an upset sale each September and December for parcels with taxes unpaid from two years earlier, plus judicial and repository sales for properties that do not sell. Buyers at an upset sale take the property subject to liens, while judicial sale parcels are offered free and clear.

If a house is behind on taxes, these are the practical paths:

  • Pay the balance and list the house normally.
  • Sell to an owner-occupant and clear the taxes from the sale proceeds.
  • Sell for cash as is to a buyer who accepts the house in its current condition.

Ask the Tax Claim Bureau for a payoff before choosing, because penalties and interest change the numbers.

faqs.q: What is the transfer tax in Montgomery Township?
faqs.a: The Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds lists the realty transfer tax at 2 percent of the sale price. The Recorder collects it when the deed is recorded, and exemptions require a Statement of Value.

faqs.q: Does the homestead exclusion transfer to the buyer?
faqs.a: No. The county removes the exclusion automatically when ownership changes, so the seller does not need to file a removal. The buyer has to apply for a new homestead exclusion on the home.

faqs.q: When is the deadline to appeal a Montgomery County assessment?
faqs.a: The annual appeal deadline is August 1 of the year before the tax year in question. The same date applies to real estate tax exemption applications.

faqs.q: Do I need a resale certificate to sell a house in Montgomery Township?
faqs.a: The township's fee schedule lists a residential Use and Occupancy permit for new construction only. Confirm with the Planning and Zoning Office at (215) 393-6920, because your buyer's lender or your association may ask for other paperwork.

faqs.q: What does Pennsylvania require sellers to disclose?
faqs.a: A seller must give the buyer a signed and dated property disclosure statement before an agreement of transfer is signed. It covers the roof, basement, structure, plumbing, heating, electrical, drainage and other known material defects.
